title: AI-DRIVEN FRAUD DETECTION AND PREVENTION USING HUMAN BEHAVIOR ANALYSIS TO ENHANCE US SOCIAL AND FINANCIAL SECURITY
authors: Islam, M. M.; Parveen, R.; Mim, S. S.; Anika, A.; Hassan, M. M.; Al Nahid, M. A.
tldr: Presents a fraud detection system combining behavioral biometrics with a mixture-of-experts architecture and drift adaptation, achieving 96.5% recall and 92.0% precision on synthetic US data.
problem_and_motivation: Existing AI-based fraud systems process events in isolation and fail to capture continuous behavioral signatures, making them vulnerable to generative AI-driven mimicry and concept drift. A system is needed that integrates temporal behavioral patterns with transaction risk to adapt to evolving fraud tactics.
approach: Extracts behavioral signals (keystroke timing, gesture trajectories, navigation transitions) from user interaction streams.
Introduces a Behavioral Trust Vectorization Engine (BTVE) that creates a per-user dynamic embedding with trust weights based on risk posture.
Uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with sequence, anomaly, and supervised experts to produce fraud probabilities.
Employs a gating network to dynamically weight expert outputs based on current behavioral and transaction context.
Monitors KL divergence, residual error, and gating shifts to detect drift and trigger retraining or BTVE resets.
Evaluates on a simulated dataset of 800,000 user sessions with 16 million event records.
Compares against transaction-only, behavior-only, fixed fusion, and hybrid MoE baselines.
findings: num: Achieved 96.5% recall, 92.0% precision, and a false positive rate below 1.6%.
num: Maintained average inference latency of approximately 8.2 ms.
num: Without adaptation, recall dropped to 89.8% after simulated mimicry; with drift adaptation, recall recovered to 95.2% within two days.
num: Gating weights averaged 42% supervised, 33% sequence, and 25% anomaly over flagged fraud events.
The system successfully detected an account takeover attempt in a real-time illustrative case.
key_figures_tables: Figure 4: Expert weight distribution across flagged fraud events → Supervised expert dominates at 42%.

key_equations.explanation: Fuses expert fraud probabilities via gating weights.
Slowly updates the stable base embedding.

definitions.definition: Behavioral Trust Vectorization Engine; maintains per-user dynamic behavioral embeddings with trust weighting.
Mixture-of-Experts; architecture combining multiple specialized models via a gating mechanism.
Kullback-Leibler divergence; measures difference between embedding distributions.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a novel algorithm for fraud detection that integrates behavioral biometrics with a mixture-of-experts and an adaptive trust-weighted embedding mechanism. It addresses the gap in handling concept drift and adversarial mimicry in real-time financial systems. The proposed Behavioral Trust Vectorization Engine provides a new formalism for dynamic, risk-sensitive user representation. The work also demonstrates a practical system design with low-latency inference suitable for deployment.
directly_justifies: Behavioral profiling can minimize false positives by differentiating genuine users from imposters.
Mixture-of-experts systems can effectively learn from noisy labels on anomaly detection tasks.
The proposed BTVE dynamically adjusts embedding reliability in response to contextual risk.
limits: The paper's findings are based on synthetic data, not real-world financial transactions.
Privacy concerns around behavioral data collection are acknowledged but not addressed algorithmically.
The system's robustness against sophisticated adversarial mimicry is not empirically validated with real attacks.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan across all topic domains was performed. The paper's primary contribution lies in algorithmic fraud detection (8.A, 8.B) using predictive modeling (6.A) with a novel MoE and embedding architecture, making these the high-relevance topics. The evaluation methodology (12.A, 12.B) and use of synthetic data (14.A) are medium-relevance supporting elements. Deployment considerations (14.B, 14.C) and privacy/user trust (10.A, 10.B) are touched upon contextually but are not the paper's focus. Topics related to Filipino demographics, financial structure, budgeting, and mobile-first design (1.A-7.E, 9.A-9.C, 13.A-13.C) were considered and rejected as the paper focuses on US fraud detection without addressing those specific domains.

limitations: Evaluation is conducted only on synthetic data, limiting generalizability to real-world financial systems. [unacknowledged]
